title: The Same Day at the Patent Office
summary: On one winter Monday in 1876, two inventors sent papers about a talking machine to the same government office in Washington. Alexander Graham Bell got the patent, and a few weeks later he spoke the first clear sentence ever heard over a telephone wire. People are still arguing about what happened in between!

sections.heading: Two Envelopes on Valentine's Day
paragraphs: Picture Washington, D.C., on the morning of Monday, February 14, 1876. It is Valentine's Day, but nobody at the United States Patent Office is thinking about cards or chocolates. The Patent Office sits inside a huge stone building with tall columns, and its halls are lined with glass cases full of little models of inventions: ploughs, sewing machines, water wheels and clever gadgets of every kind. Clerks scratch away with steel pens. Lawyers in dark coats come and go, carrying envelopes stuffed with drawings and long, careful descriptions.
Two of those envelopes, delivered that day, would become some of the most argued-about pieces of paper in the history of invention.

One came from Alexander Graham Bell, the 28-year-old Boston teacher of deaf students whom we met in Part 6. It was a full application for a patent, titled “Improvement in Telegraphy.” It described Bell's ideas for sending several telegraph messages at once using musical tones, but tucked inside it was something much bigger: a method for sending “vocal or other sounds” along a wire by making the electric current rise and fall in the same pattern as the sound itself. In other words, it described a way to send a human voice.

The other envelope came from Elisha Gray, the experienced Chicago inventor and co-founder of the company that became Western Electric, whom we met in Part 5. Gray was not asking for a patent yet. He was filing a caveat, a kind of official notice that said, in effect, “I am working on this invention and I plan to patent it soon.” His caveat had a long title: “Instruments for Transmitting and Receiving Vocal Sounds Telegraphically.” It included a drawing of a person speaking into a cone-shaped mouthpiece above a small container of liquid. That design is called a liquid transmitter, and we will see exactly how it works later in this chapter.

So on the very same day, two inventors who barely knew each other told the same government office that they had found a way to make electricity talk. It sounds almost like a made-up story. But it really happened, and the papers still exist in archives today.
Bell's application had actually been ready for weeks. So why had it not been filed sooner?

The reason was money and a bit of international planning. Bell had made a deal with George Brown, a Canadian newspaper owner and politician from Toronto, who agreed to help pay for a British patent. Patent rules in Britain at that time could refuse a patent for an invention that had already been made public somewhere else. So Bell's side wanted Brown to file in Britain first, before the American patent was published. Brown sailed to England carrying a copy of Bell's description, but he was slow to act, and some accounts say he worried that British experts would think the idea was silly.

Meanwhile, Bell's main backer in Boston, Gardiner Greene Hubbard, was growing impatient. Hubbard was a lawyer and businessman, and he was also the father of Mabel Hubbard, the young woman Bell hoped to marry. Hubbard understood patents well, and he knew that other inventors, especially Elisha Gray, were working on very similar musical telegraph ideas. Every week of waiting was a week in which someone else might get there first.

In the end, Hubbard decided not to wait for Brown. Bell's patent lawyers in Washington, Anthony Pollok and Marcellus Bailey, had the application ready, and it was delivered by hand to the Patent Office on February 14. Bell himself was in Boston at the time. Some accounts say Hubbard sent the application in without asking Bell first, which would show how nervous his backers were about the race.

It is worth pausing on how much depended on this one decision. If Hubbard had waited even a few more days, Gray's caveat would have been sitting in the office alone, and the story of the telephone might have been told very differently.

sections.heading: Patents and Caveats: The Rules of the Race
paragraphs: To understand why people still argue about February 14, 1876, you need to know what a patent and a caveat actually were.

A patent is a government document that gives an inventor the right to control their invention for a set time. In the United States in 1876, a patent lasted 17 years. During that time, nobody else was allowed to make, use or sell the invention without the patent owner's permission. In return, the inventor had to explain the invention clearly in writing, with drawings, so that after the patent ran out, anyone could use the idea. A patent is a kind of deal: the inventor shares the secret, and the government protects it for a while.

Getting a patent was not automatic. A government worker called an examiner read each application and checked whether the idea was new and whether anyone else had claimed something similar. If two people seemed to claim the same invention, the examiner could declare an interference, which was like calling a time-out so the Patent Office could figure out who had really invented it first.

A caveat was something smaller. It was an old type of US patent office notice, now no longer used, that an inventor could file when an invention was not quite finished. It cost only a small fee, about 10 dollars, and lasted for one year. The caveat was kept secret. Its main power was this: if someone else applied for a patent on something that clashed with the caveat during that year, the Patent Office was supposed to warn the person who filed the caveat, and give them about three months to send in a full application of their own.

There was one more very important rule. In 1876, the United States gave patents to the first person to invent something, not simply to the first person whose papers reached the office. (The US only switched to a mostly “first to file” system in the 2010s.) That means the hour of arrival was not supposed to decide everything by itself. But it still mattered a great deal, because it affected whether Gray's caveat could block Bell's application or force a contest between them. That is why the order of the two envelopes became such a big deal.

sections.heading: Who Got There First?
paragraphs: Here is where the story gets tangled. Nobody wrote down the exact minute each envelope came through the door, so historians have had to piece the day together from office records and from what people said years later, often in court.

What seems clear is that Gray signed his caveat and had it notarized (officially stamped by a witness) in Washington that Monday morning, and his patent lawyer, William D. Baldwin, took it to the Patent Office. Bell's lawyer, Marcellus Bailey, delivered Bell's application by hand, probably shortly before noon.

But arriving at the building was not the same as being officially recorded. The office kept a “cash blotter,” a daily list of fees paid. Bell's fee was written down early in the day; one account says his application was the fifth entry. Gray's caveat, according to many accounts, sat in a basket of incoming papers and was not entered until later that afternoon, far down the list. So on paper, Bell's application looked like it came first, even if Gray's lawyer may have walked through the door earlier.

Gray himself changed his mind about this over the years. At first he wrote that he had been “an hour or two behind” Bell. Later, after years of lawsuits had dug up more evidence, he became convinced that his caveat had actually arrived first. To this day, the honest answer is that which one arrived first is still debated.

What happened next is better documented. On February 19, five days after the filings, the patent examiner, Zenas Fisk Wilber, read both documents. He noticed that one idea in Bell's application, using a changing resistance to make the current copy a sound wave, also appeared in Gray's caveat. Following the rules, Wilber suspended Bell's application for three months so that Gray would have time to file a full application if he wanted to.

Bell's lawyers protested. They argued that Bell's application had been received first, so the caveat should not count against it. The Patent Office agreed, and the suspension was lifted. Bell then travelled from Boston to Washington in late February and met Wilber in person. What exactly the two men talked about in that meeting would later become the most controversial part of the whole story, as we will see.

Gray, meanwhile, did not rush to file a full application. He seems to have believed, like many telegraph experts, that the real money was in sending many telegraph messages at once, not in a talking toy. That decision would cost him dearly.

sections.heading: Patent Number 174,465
paragraphs: On March 7, 1876, the United States Patent Office issued Patent No. 174,465 to Alexander Graham Bell of Salem, Massachusetts. (Bell often stayed with the Sanders family in Salem, which is why that town is printed on the patent.) Its official title was still “Improvement in Telegraphy.” Nothing on the front page shouted the word “telephone.”

The patent was only a few pages long, with a couple of sheets of drawings. Much of it describes ways to send several musical tones down one wire. But near the end come the claims, the numbered sentences that say exactly what the inventor owns. Claim 4 describes making “undulations,” which means smooth waves, in a continuous electric current by gradually increasing and decreasing the resistance of the circuit. Resistance is how hard it is for electricity to flow through something. Change the resistance smoothly, and the current changes smoothly too.

Claim 5 is the famous one. It claims the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically by causing “electrical undulations, similar in form to the vibrations of the air” that go with the sound. In everyday words: make the electric current wiggle in exactly the same shape as the sound wave, send it down the wire, and turn it back into sound at the other end. That is the basic idea of every telephone that worked on wires for the next hundred years.

There was something strange about this patent, though. When it was granted, Bell had not yet made a device that sent clear spoken words. He had heard the twang of a reed in June 1875, and he and Watson had heard faint voice-like sounds with their “gallows” instrument that summer. But no one had yet heard a full, understandable sentence. The patent described a principle and some instruments that should work, rather than a finished, tested product. Patent law allowed this, as long as the description was clear enough.

Because Claim 5 was written so broadly, it covered almost any way of sending speech by an electric current that copied the sound wave. That made it fantastically valuable. Over the next years Bell's company would use it to defend its business in hundreds of court cases, which you will read about in Part 10. Patent 174,465 is often called one of the most valuable patents ever issued.

sections.heading: How a Liquid Transmitter Works
paragraphs: Before we get to the big moment, let's look at the strange device that made it possible. It is called a liquid transmitter, or sometimes a water transmitter.

Imagine a small metal cup filled with water that has a little acid mixed in. Acid makes water carry electricity much better than pure water would. A wire from a battery is connected to the cup. Above the cup hangs a stretched sheet of thin material called a diaphragm, a bit like the skin of a drum. A thin metal needle or wire is fixed to the middle of the diaphragm and dips just slightly into the liquid. A second wire runs from that needle out to the line and on to the receiver in the other room.

Now speak into a mouthpiece aimed at the diaphragm. Your voice is made of quick pushes and pulls in the air. Each push nudges the diaphragm down, so the needle sinks a tiny bit deeper into the acid water. Each pull lets the diaphragm rise, and the needle comes up a little. When the needle is deeper, the electricity has a wider, shorter path through the liquid, so the resistance drops and more current flows. When it rises, the resistance goes up and less current flows.

The result is wonderful: the current in the wire now rises and falls in the same pattern as your voice. Bell's own patent described the idea this way: the more deeply a wire is dipped in the liquid, the less resistance the liquid offers to the current.

At the far end, that wobbling current flows through an electromagnet, a coil of wire that becomes a magnet when electricity flows through it. The stronger the current, the harder the magnet pulls on a thin piece of iron or a reed nearby. As the current wobbles, the iron shakes back and forth, pushing the air and recreating the sound. You will learn much more about receivers in Part 9.

The liquid transmitter had big problems. The acid could spill, the needle had to be adjusted very carefully, and the sound was weak. It was a great tool for proving an idea in a laboratory, but not something you would want in your living room. That is why neither Bell nor anyone else used it in telephones that were sold to the public.

sections.heading: Mr. Watson, Come Here
paragraphs: Now we arrive at the most famous moment in telephone history.

It is Friday, March 10, 1876, three days after the patent was granted. Bell and his assistant, Thomas Watson, are working in Bell's rented rooms in Boston. Most accounts place them at 5 Exeter Place, where Bell lived and kept a small workshop. The transmitter, a liquid transmitter much like the one we just described, is in one room. The receiver is in another room, with the door closed between them. A wire runs from one to the other.
Watson waits in the receiving room with his ear pressed to the instrument. Bell leans over the transmitter in the other room and speaks into the mouthpiece.

That evening, Bell wrote about the experiment in his laboratory notebook. His entry describes how the receiving instrument was set up in one room and the transmitting instrument in another, and then says that he shouted into the mouthpiece: “Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you.” Bell wrote that, to his delight, Watson came, and declared that he had heard and understood what Bell said.

Notice the exact words. Many books and films say Bell called “Mr. Watson, come here, I need you,” but that is not what his notebook records. The written wording, in Bell's own hand, is “Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you.” Watson, writing his memories many years later, remembered it slightly differently, which is normal for human memory. That is why historians trust the notebook, written that same day, more than stories told decades afterwards.

Bell's notebook goes on. He asked Watson to repeat the words, and Watson did. Then they swapped places. Bell listened at the receiver while Watson read passages from a book into the transmitter. Bell wrote that he could definitely hear speech sounds coming from the receiver, though they were loud but muffled and not always clear. He could make out some words, but not every one.

There is also a well-known story, told by Watson in his autobiography published in 1926, that Bell called for him because he had spilled some of the battery acid on his clothes. It makes a fun scene, but it does not appear in Bell's notebook entry for that day, so it is best to treat it as a later memory rather than a certain fact. Whatever the reason for calling, the important thing is that the message got through.

Bell was thrilled. In a letter to his father written around this time, he said he felt he had at last found the solution to a great problem, and he imagined a day when wires would run into houses like water or gas pipes, so that friends could talk to each other without leaving home. The notebook from that day is now kept in the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., as part of the Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, and you can see scans of the pages online.

sections.heading: A Fair Look at the Big Argument
paragraphs: Now for the hard question that has followed Bell for 150 years. The transmitter that worked on March 10 used a needle dipped in acid water to change resistance. That is very similar to the drawing in Elisha Gray's caveat. And just two days earlier, on March 8, Bell's notebook had included a sketch of a liquid transmitter that looks a lot like Gray's drawing. Did Bell see Gray's papers?
Here are the pieces of evidence, laid out as fairly as possible.

First, the patent examiner. Ten years later, in 1886, Zenas Wilber signed a sworn statement saying that during Bell's visit in February 1876 he had shown Bell Gray's caveat drawing, and that Bell had given him money. Bell strongly denied this under oath. Wilber's story was not as solid as it sounds: in 1885 he had signed an earlier statement that said the opposite, and he was described as a heavy drinker who owed money to Bell's lawyer, Marcellus Bailey. His 1886 statement was also prepared with the help of lawyers for a rival company that was being sued by Bell's company. So both his statements are hard to trust.

Second, the margin note. In Bell's patent application there is a short passage about variable resistance in liquid that appears to have been added in the margin. Bell's supporters say this was his own idea, written before the filing. Some writers on Gray's side argue that it was added later. In 1879, Bell himself testified that Wilber had discussed Gray's caveat with him “in a general way” during the visit.

Third, Bell's earlier work. Bell's supporters point out that he had already been experimenting with variable resistance ideas, and that in the summer of 1875 he had heard sounds through his instruments. They argue that he understood the principle on his own, and that testing a liquid transmitter after the patent was granted was simply a sensible experiment.

Historians still disagree. In 2000, A. Edward Evenson argued in a book that Gray's idea may have leaked to Bell's lawyers, perhaps without Bell even knowing. In 2008, the journalist Seth Shulman argued in his book The Telephone Gambit that Bell did borrow from Gray's caveat. Other historians, including Bell's major biographer Robert V. Bruce, defended Bell and doubted Wilber's honesty. The courts of the time, after years of lawsuits, always ruled in Bell's favour. The Patent Office decided that although Gray may have been first to describe the variable-resistance idea, he had lost his claim by not acting on it until after others had shown it worked.

So what should you believe? The fairest answer is this: it has never been proven that Bell copied Gray, and it has never been completely disproven either. What we can say for sure is that both men were brilliant, both were working on the same problem at the same time, and both were building on the ideas of earlier people like Reis and Meucci. Inventions rarely spring from just one head.

sections.heading: A Patent, a Device, and a Big Question
paragraphs: By the middle of March 1876, Bell had two things almost nobody else in the world had: a United States patent covering the transmission of speech by electricity, and a working machine that had carried a whole sentence from one room to another.

But a machine that whispers through a closed door is not yet a world-changing invention. The sound was faint. The transmitter used a cup of acid. The wire was only a few metres long. To most people in 1876, the idea of talking through a wire sounded either like magic or like a parlour trick, a fun gadget to show guests at a party.

Bell and Watson quickly set to work making better instruments. Within months they had built new transmitters that used magnets and coils instead of acid, so they did not need any liquid at all. These magneto instruments were weaker but much simpler, and they could work as both a mouthpiece and an earpiece.

And Elisha Gray? He went on to have a long and successful career. He kept inventing, and in 1888 he patented the telautograph, a machine that could send handwriting over wires, an early ancestor of the fax machine. He died in 1901. He never stopped believing that he had been treated unfairly in the telephone story.

Bell, meanwhile, now faced a brand-new challenge, one that had nothing to do with wires or magnets. He held a patent and a working device. But he still needed to convince the world, from scientists and emperors to businessmen and ordinary families, that a talking wire was much more than a toy.

deepDive: The events of February and March 1876 sit at the centre of one of the longest-running disputes in the history of technology, and it is worth understanding why the evidence is so slippery. Under the US law of the time, patents were awarded on a first-to-invent basis, so the order in which papers reached the Patent Office was not in itself decisive. What mattered procedurally was whether Gray's caveat would trigger an interference against Bell's application. Patent examiner Zenas Fisk Wilber initially suspended Bell's application on February 19 for three months because Bell's claim about variable resistance overlapped Gray's caveat; Bell's attorneys argued that their application had been received first, and the suspension was withdrawn. Patent 174,465 issued on March 7. The disputed points are: when each document was actually received (office records show Bell's fee recorded earlier, while some accounts say Gray's caveat sat uncatalogued in an in-basket); whether a short passage on liquid variable resistance in Bell's application was added after his lawyers learned of Gray's caveat; and what passed between Bell and Wilber during Bell's late-February visit. Wilber gave contradictory sworn statements in 1885 and 1886, and the later one, alleging he showed Bell the caveat and received money, was drafted with lawyers for the Pan-Electric Telephone Company, a rival being sued by Bell. Bell denied the accusations under oath. Bell's notebook sketch of March 8 and the March 10 liquid transmitter strongly resemble Gray's caveat drawing, which is the core of the case made by writers such as A. Edward Evenson (2000) and Seth Shulman (2008). Bell's defenders, including biographer Robert V. Bruce, note Bell's earlier variable-resistance thinking and argue the March experiment was a proof of principle for a claim already made. Importantly, the liquid transmitter was a technological dead end: Bell's public demonstrations used magneto instruments, and practical telephones adopted carbon transmitters, which also work by variable resistance. Courts consistently upheld Bell's patent. Most historians today treat the question of copying as unresolved, while agreeing that several inventors were converging on electrical speech at the same moment.
funFact: Bell's famous telephone patent, No. 174,465, never uses the word “telephone” in its title; it is officially called “Improvement in Telegraphy.”

check.q: What did Bell say into the transmitter on March 10, 1876, according to his own notebook?
check.a: Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you
wrong: Mr. Watson, come here, I need you
